items.title: Waydroid starts but eth0 never gets IPv4 address, no DHCP lease, no network connectivity
items.body:
## Summary

Waydroid starts normally, but Android never gets an IPv4 address on `eth0`, so there is no network connectivity.

This reproduces after:

- full reinitialization
- switching from current images to older images
- downgrading Waydroid from `1.6.2` to `1.6.1` and `1.6.0`

## Environment

- Host OS: Ubuntu 24.04.1
- Kernel: `Linux 6.17.0-20-generic #20~24.04.1-Ubuntu SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Thu Mar 19 01:28:37 UTC 2026 x86_64`
- Architecture: `x86_64`
- Waydroid versions tested: `1.6.2`, `1.6.1`, `1.6.0`
- Current display session: Wayland
- Host uplink: `eno1` ethernet

## What happens

- `waydroid0` is created correctly on the host
- `waydroid0` has `192.168.240.1/24`
- `dnsmasq` starts and binds to `waydroid0`
- `iptables-legacy` has INPUT/FORWARD/MASQUERADE rules for `waydroid0`
- Android `eth0` is `UP`, but never gets an IPv4 address
- `/var/lib/misc/dnsmasq.waydroid0.leases` stays empty
- `ip route` inside Waydroid is empty

## Reproduction

1. Install Waydroid on Ubuntu 24.04.1 x86_64.
2. Start the container and launch the full UI.
3. Check network state inside Waydroid.

## Diagnostics

Host:

```bash
$ ip addr show waydroid0
26: waydroid0: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc noqueue state UP group default qlen 1000
    link/ether <redacted> brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
    inet 192.168.240.1/24 brd 192.168.240.255 scope global waydroid0
```

```bash
$ nmcli device status
DEVICE      TYPE      STATE            CONNECTION
eno1        ethernet  connected        netplan-eno1
lo          loopback  connected (externally)  lo
lxcbr0      bridge    connected (externally)  lxcbr0
waydroid0   bridge    unmanaged        --
```

```bash
$ sudo iptables-legacy -S INPUT
-P INPUT ACCEPT
-A INPUT -i waydroid0 -p tcp -m tcp --dport 53 -j ACCEPT
-A INPUT -i waydroid0 -p udp -m udp --dport 53 -j ACCEPT
-A INPUT -i waydroid0 -p tcp -m tcp --dport 67 -j ACCEPT
-A INPUT -i waydroid0 -p udp -m udp --dport 67 -j ACCEPT
```

```bash
$ sudo iptables-legacy -S FORWARD
-P FORWARD ACCEPT
-A FORWARD -o waydroid0 -j ACCEPT
-A FORWARD -i waydroid0 -j ACCEPT
```

```bash
$ sudo iptables-legacy -t nat -S
-P PREROUTING ACCEPT
-P INPUT ACCEPT
-P OUTPUT ACCEPT
-P POSTROUTING ACCEPT
-A POSTROUTING -s 192.168.240.0/24 ! -d 192.168.240.0/24 -j MASQUERADE
```

```bash
$ sudo ss -ulpn | grep dnsmasq
UNCONN 0      0      0.0.0.0%waydroid0:67         0.0.0.0:*    users:(("dnsmasq",pid=...,fd=4))
UNCONN 0      0          192.168.240.1:53         0.0.0.0:*    users:(("dnsmasq",pid=...,fd=6))
```

Inside Waydroid:

```bash
$ sudo waydroid shell ip addr
1: lo: <LOOPBACK,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 65536 qdisc noqueue state UNKNOWN group default qlen 1000
2: eth0@if37: <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP> mtu 1500 qdisc noqueue state UP group default qlen 1000
    link/ether <redacted> brd ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff link-netnsid 0
    inet6 <redacted>/64 scope link stable-privacy
```

```bash
$ sudo waydroid shell ip route
# empty
```

```bash
$ sudo cat /var/lib/misc/dnsmasq.waydroid0.leases
# empty
```

`tcpdump` on `waydroid0` captured a DHCP discover at least once:

```text
0.0.0.0.68 > 255.255.255.255.67: BOOTP/DHCP, Request ..., DHCP-Message (53): Discover
```

but no corresponding lease was created and Android still got no IPv4 address.

## Things already tried

- switched from X11 to Wayland
- full Waydroid reinit multiple times
- removed `/var/lib/waydroid`
- tested official current images and older images
- downgraded Waydroid package from `1.6.2` to `1.6.1` and `1.6.0`
- marked `waydroid0` as unmanaged in NetworkManager
- confirmed host forwarding and NAT are enabled
- restarted `waydroid-container` and `waydroid-net.sh`

## Expected result

Waydroid should obtain an IPv4 address on `eth0`, receive a default route via `192.168.240.1`, and have working network connectivity.

items.title: feat(credentials): allocate isolated browser network namespaces
items.body:
## What changed or was removed

Add Root-only private network allocation to credential browser supervision. The namespace contains only loopback and one non-reusable TCP proxy listener; socket namespace evidence must match the new namespace. Setup restores its dedicated Go OS thread before publishing descriptors, discards the thread if restoration fails, and cleans late cancellation results. Borrowing duplicates protected descriptors; close denies further borrowing. Non-Linux setup denies.

## Why

The browser needs a kernel network boundary before receiving passwords. A proxy flag alone permits direct networking bypass. Serving an inherited private-namespace listener lets the broker enforce HTTP and lease policy while using its own normal network namespace for approved HTTPS upstream connections; the browser has no external route.

## User and developer impact

This is a startup resource prerequisite in the existing private supervision package. It creates no bridge, veth, external route, DNS service or host firewall rule. Main does not call it and no SDK, token or credential intent endpoint is activated. Borrowed descriptors remain the caller's responsibility: full teardown must close the proxy/accepted sockets, retire the forest and release borrowed pins. The full launcher and authenticated Root supervision transport remain later work.

## Validation

- Native package race tests, Linux cross-compilation, full Linux lint, `make fmt`/`make fmt-check`, documentation lint, shell syntax and diff checks pass.
- Actual Linux fixtures verify a distinct namespace, original Go namespace restoration, outside-broker listener adoption, a synthetic byte from the isolated namespace, kernel denial of direct external IPv4/IPv6 connections, unprivileged setup denial, canceled borrowing, repeated allocation/cleanup and closed-resource denial.
- A separate child exhausts descriptor allocation after unshare and verifies failed setup does not contaminate Go namespace state. No parent limits are changed.
- The combined forest/network fixture passes normally and under the race detector on a bounded disposable Root systemd unit with a private parent network namespace and empty environment. Supplemental standalone race compilation uses Go 1.26.6 and repository x/sys v0.48.0. Temporary units, namespaces and public files are removed.
- Extend the mandatory PR qualification script to both race-enabled fixtures; retain the complete forest-death/quarantine cases and require an explicit PASS for each. CI must pass on the published head before merge.

## Later PRs

Build the fixed Root launcher with protected role/configuration, immutable runtime mounting, PID/filesystem namespaces, privilege dropping and authenticated private broker IPC; pair the network and forest with the actual enforcing proxy and original lease. Protected Mac/VM hosting, remote agent intents, physical Android/notifications and the real-site pilot remain unqualified. A real token must remain outside chat and model-visible tooling.

items.title: Core implementation: conservative per-connection MTU selection
items.body:
# Result

Implemented conservative, default-on, per-connection MTU selection in Porta 0.1.6. Wire protocol remains version 2: this is an explicitly negotiated optional extension. The development server and all six client downloads are now deployed at https://porta-dev.i-csu.org:8443. Source is not yet committed, pushed, or published as a GitHub release.

## Chosen policy

- Automatic MTU is now the development default, with a 1400 ceiling and conservative 1100 baseline. This supersedes the initial opt-in policy and is active on the development endpoint.
- The daemon, deployment script, bundled unit and network helper use consistent automatic defaults. Use `--auto-mtu=false --mtu 1100` for a fixed MTU. Generated units pass the selected mode explicitly to both the daemon and helper.
- `--mtu` remains the shared gateway TUN MTU and sets the automatic ceiling.
- Clients require no extra switch. Discovery applies only to native HTTP/3 connections with HTTP Datagrams enabled at both ends.
- Select before address assignment and interface configuration; do not continuously resize a live TUN.
- Start at 1100. Raise only after receiving a same-size, authenticated datagram echo proving current delivery in both directions.
- Probe only up to the lesser of the configured ceiling and 1400, with a 750 ms total budget and at most two 150 ms attempts per candidate. Keep the last confirmed value or 1100 when inconclusive.
- Selection runs again on reconnect. Existing desktop reconfiguration handles changed lease MTUs; a change may interrupt existing flows.
- HTTP/2, Android's four-lane HTTP/2 fallback, and HTTP/3 without Datagrams retain the configured MTU.
- The HTTPS forward proxy is unaffected; it has no VPN TUN interface.

## Protocol and failure handling

- `X-Porta-MTU-Discovery: 1` requests the capability. An eligible server returns a fresh session nonce in that header.
- Context ID 1 probes occupy exactly the same number of HTTP Datagram bytes as a Context ID 0 IP packet of the proposed MTU. Nonce, sequence, declared size and padding are validated.
- The server echoes only actual unreliable datagrams, with a bounded probe quota and expiry. A reliable DATAGRAM capsule can never prove datagram support.
- Reliable `MTU_SELECT`/`MTU_SELECTED` capsules agree on the final MTU before ADDRESS_REQUEST. Unproven higher selections, wrong nonces, and live MTU changes are rejected.
- Missing or malformed reliable agreement cannot return a partially configured connection and does not justify transport downgrade.
- The existing overall startup timeout still covers discovery and agreement.
- Normal IP packets still fall back to a reliable capsule on `quic.DatagramTooLargeError`, including if QUIC's current size limit later shrinks. Smaller packets keep the datagram path.

## Per-client gateway handling

- Each MASQUE session enforces its own selected MTU without shrinking the shared TUN for other clients.
- Downlink IP traffic is withheld until address assignment completes.
- Oversized DF-clear IPv4 packets are fragmented, preserving payload, identification, fragment offsets/MF, copied options and correct header checksums. Re-fragmentation is supported.
- Oversized DF-set packets receive ICMP Destination Unreachable / Fragmentation Needed, advertising the selected MTU and quoting the original header plus eight bytes. Feedback is injected into gateway TUN toward the original sender.
- Invalid headers and forbidden ICMP cases are dropped explicitly; valid ICMP feedback is limited to one per 100 ms per session.
- Linux normally rejects locally sourced TUN ingress. The auto-MTU network helper explicitly sets `accept_local=1` and loose `rp_filter=2` on the owned TUN only. Global and physical-interface RPF settings are not changed. The required `mtu_feedback` readiness check rejects unusable local-source/RPF configuration; no production raw-socket capability is added.
- Ordinary fitting packets retain the no-payload-copy path. MTU lookup uses an atomic load rather than a packet-path lock.
- Server logs report selected MTUs. `porta_mtu_packets_total` reports fragmented, ICMP-sent, suppressed and rate-limited outcomes.

## Evidence

- Deterministic tests cover asymmetric forward/reverse limits, local payload-limit errors, loss, retries, stale nonce/sequence, budget expiry, cancellation, send/receive errors, exact ceiling selection, probe quotas and expiry.
- Control tests reject unproven selection, wrong acknowledgement/token, assignment before MTU agreement, and in-session size changes. Capsule-carried probes do not confirm datagram delivery.
- IPv4 tests cover checksums, options, fragmentation/re-fragmentation, maximum sizes, source immutability, DF, ICMP suppression and malformed input. The helper implementation also passed a 471,091-execution fuzz run.
- Gateway tests exercise different per-session MTUs, ingress enforcement, reassembled downlink payloads, ICMP routing/rate limiting, ordinary-packet continuity and I/O-error propagation.
- A real Linux network-namespace regression uses native TUN, veth, the production network helper and real conntrack SNAT/DNAT. It reproduces the successful-TUN-write-but-no-ICMP-egress failure with local-source rejection, and the strict-RPF/loopback-reverse-route case. After the scoped helper settings, it captures checksum-valid ICMP type 3/code 4 on WAN, verifies MTU 1100 and NAT translation of both outer and quoted headers, while global and physical RPF stay strict.
- The native regression passed three race-enabled runs. `make test-native-mtu` runs it only inside a fresh isolated network namespace; the test refuses PID 1's namespace and namespaces with existing non-loopback interfaces. Linux CI invokes this target explicitly.
- Real local HTTP/3 tests negotiate MTU, transfer selected-size uploads, fragment shared-TUN downlink packets, produce DF feedback, and continue ordinary traffic without changing the lease MTU.
- Ten repeated real-transport runs passed, observing setup-time selections of 1200 and 1400 under a 1500 server ceiling. This demonstrates why discovery is a current conservative observation, not a promise to find the absolute maximum.
- Fixed mode, disabled Datagrams, an explicitly capped 1100 MTU, the default 1400 ceiling, and HTTP/2 configured-MTU behavior have real transport regressions. The prior `20 -> 8000 -> 20` bidirectional fixed-mode regression remains passing.
- Targeted protocol, MASQUE, gateway, tunnel, client lifecycle, mobile bridge, server and CLI race tests and vet passed.
- Daemon flag tests and isolated deployment tests cover automatic defaults, custom ceilings and fixed-mode overrides. The native regression exercises the helper's automatic default. Source remains 0.1.6.
- Linux binaries and Windows AMD64 GUI/CLI/ZIP were rebuilt; Windows ARM64 client test compilation and scoped AMD64/ARM64 vet passed. Android's native Go bridge was forcibly rebuilt, all 20 Android unit tests passed, and all three release APKs were produced.

## Local deployment acceptance (2026-09-05)

- Upgraded the development server from 0.1.4 to 0.1.6 using the existing rollback-capable deployment script. Existing credentials, accounts, TLS configuration, pool and egress settings were preserved.
- Published Linux AMD64/ARM64, Windows AMD64 ZIP, and all three Android APKs as 0.1.6, together with their checksum manifest and client-version metadata. Publication exchanged the complete download directory atomically; previous binaries/configuration/downloads remain available in a private local rollback backup.
- All required readiness components report healthy, including `mtu_feedback`. The shared server TUN is 1400; global and physical-interface RPF retained their previous values.
- Real public-endpoint HTTP/3 connections negotiated 1280 and 1360 MTUs. The final acceptance run carried 1360-byte kernel ICMP echoes in both directions and Internet DNS queries before/after. HTTP/2 retained 1400 and carried matching full-size echoes and Internet DNS.
- Authenticated HTTPS CONNECT proxying carried real HTTPS Internet traffic.
- Signed into the public download portal with a temporary client account and downloaded all six published artifacts; every HTTP-delivered SHA-256 matched the staged manifest. Temporary probe accounts were removed afterward.
- Padded UDP DNS was not used as the full-MTU oracle: the public resolver also timed out for those requests sent directly outside Porta. Full-size kernel echoes and separate normal Internet DNS checks were used instead.
- Android artifacts use the local development signing key because release signing credentials are not configured. This key differs from the previous portal APK's key: an installation from that previous APK requires uninstall/reinstall rather than an in-place update. Save profile/token details before uninstalling.

## Boundaries

This does not replace QUIC's outer path-MTU discovery, guarantee delivery after arbitrary path changes, or guarantee remote hosts honor ICMP. Shrinking an inner MTU cannot fix a path unable to carry QUIC's minimum UDP packet size. Capsule fallback retains stream head-of-line blocking for affected packets.

For VPN-over-VPN, 1100 is not a universal guarantee: QUIC needs the outer tunnel to carry at least a 1200-byte UDP payload (at least 1228 bytes with IPv4 or 1248 with IPv6 before options/extension headers). An outer VPN MTU of 1100 cannot carry that unfragmented minimum; HTTP/2/TCP is the appropriate fallback where available. Routing and firewall/kill-switch compatibility must also permit the nested tunnel.

Native Windows BFE/GUI/packet-level acceptance remains a separate item in #5; Linux-hosted cross-builds are not native Windows execution. Development deployment acceptance is complete; source publication and a GitHub release remain outstanding, so this issue remains open.

Implementation: `internal/masque/mtu.go`, `internal/tunnel/mtu.go`, `internal/gateway/mtu.go`, `internal/protocol/mtu.go`, and transport integration. Operator/protocol/client details are documented in README and `docs/{architecture,clients,deployment,endpoints,threat-model}.md`. Related transport recovery work: #4.

items.title: Give native Docker containers IPv4 internet access
items.body:
The native Docker launcher created a private network namespace with no uplink, so containers and the daemon could not reach the internet. It now connects that namespace to Android's IPv4 connection through a supervised veth uplink. Registry pulls, DNS, HTTP(S), and package downloads work on default and user-created Docker bridges.

The supervisor follows Android root's selected internet routing table, blocks egress when no route is available, and restores connectivity when it returns. Its forwarding request is managed by netd; firewall and policy changes are scoped to the Docker uplink and removed after daemon exit or explicit stop. The daemon trusts Android's system CA directories. The original offline mode remains available with `--isolated`.

Validated on SM-A515F / A515FXXU5EUJ4 with SELinux Enforcing:

- A real `alpine:3.22` download from Docker Hub on the handset.
- External DNS, IPv4 HTTP, certificate-verified HTTPS, rejection of an untrusted certificate, and `apk update` on both bridge types.
- Container-name DNS and bridge round trip; an internal bridge remains offline.
- Daemon restart, automatic recovery after route loss, duplicate-start rejection, supervisor-kill recovery, and automatic/explicit cleanup. Android firewall rules, policy rules, and forwarding state matched their baseline after cleanup.
- KVM: 12 guest cycles across all eight CPUs, held-vCPU idle/migration, and virtual timers on CPU0/CPU4.
- `make check`, ShellCheck, Python compilation, and `git diff --check`.

Sanitized results are in `evidence/docker-internet-summary.json`; reproduction instructions and the internet validator are included. Wi-Fi was measured. This uplink does not add container IPv6, LAN ingress, per-app VPN policy, or an autostart service.

items.title: Add interface / source-IP binding for connections (#2286)
items.body:
Engine side of the interface binding requested in rustdesk/rustdesk#2286. The UI/wiring half is rustdesk/rustdesk#15675.

**Off by default** — existing installs behave exactly as before until the option is set.

## What it does

Binds sockets to a chosen network interface or source IP, for incoming and outgoing connections. The motivating case: after sleep/wake with a VPN up, the VPN owns the default route, so RustDesk registers and listens via the VPN and the host is no longer reachable on the LAN.

**One option**, `bind-interface`: a source address when the value parses as one, an interface name otherwise — the rule libtorrent uses for `outgoing_interfaces`. An interface name *also* pins the socket to the device, so egress follows it regardless of the routing table:

- Linux/Android — `SO_BINDTODEVICE`
- macOS/iOS — `IP_BOUND_IF`
- Windows — `IP_UNICAST_IF` (IPv6 uses the adapter's IPv6 scope id, not the IPv4 interface index)

Interface names are resolved to the system device name first, since `if_nametoindex` and `SO_BINDTODEVICE` do not accept friendly names such as macOS `Wi-Fi`.

**Anything unusable falls back** to letting the OS choose: an interface that is gone, or one with no address of the requested family. The device is only pinned when the same decision produced a source address, so pinning can never contradict the fallback. There is no fail-closed mode — per the discussion in this PR, a remote-access tool that refuses to connect can lock you out of the machine you needed it for.

## Scope

Covered: outgoing connections (rendezvous, relay, direct peer), the direct-access listener, the direct UDP setup path *and its reachability probe*, and the WebSocket transport, which dials through a socket we bind rather than letting tungstenite open an unbound one.

Deliberately **not** pinned: sockets whose local address came from the caller rather than from this configuration — `new_listener` (the port-forward and RDP listeners on `127.0.0.1`), `FramedStream::new` with an explicit `local_addr`, and `FramedSocket::new/new_reuse`. `SO_BINDTODEVICE` on those would filter out traffic that used to arrive fine.

Not covered: the WebRTC transport and the SOCKS/HTTP proxy path, which have their own connection code.

## Changes

- `src/config.rs` — the option, the decision logic, `get_bind_source_ip`, `get_bind_listen_ip`, `get_bind_device`, `apply_bind_device`, `bind_socket_to_interface`
- `src/tcp.rs`, `src/udp.rs` — apply the binding, with an explicit `pin_device` flag so only our own addresses are pinned
- `src/socket_client.rs` — the direct UDP path and its probe
- `src/websocket.rs` — dial through a bound, pinned socket
- `Cargo.toml` — `netdev` 0.37 (newest release still on edition 2021, so the declared Rust 1.75 keeps working), aliased to `netif` to avoid clashing with the existing `rustdesk-org/default_net` fork
- `tests/bind_interface.rs` — loopback integration tests

## Testing

`cargo test`: 108 unit + 5 integration pass. `socket_client::tests::test_nat64` fails here but fails identically on a clean `main` — it needs working IPv6 to nip.io.

Against **real interfaces** in network namespaces (two veth pairs into separate namespaces plus a dummy carrying a full-tunnel default route), 14/14. The VPN case is checked with negative controls: with no route to the target except the blackhole default, an unbound socket fails **and a source-IP binding alone fails**, so only real device pinning can get through — and both the TCP and the WebSocket path do. That harness is local; it is not part of this PR.

Per-platform socket options were type-checked for `x86_64-pc-windows-gnu`, `aarch64-apple-darwin`, `aarch64-apple-ios`, `aarch64-linux-android` and Linux by lifting the platform block into a scratch crate — a full `cargo check` per target is blocked here by C dependencies. **Runtime behaviour on Windows/macOS/iOS is unverified**; the Windows IPv6 scope id in particular is a change I could not execute.
